## Setup

Index rows 1 (north) to 8 (south), columns 1 (west) to 8 (east). A house at cell $(r,c)$ is **in the shade** iff cells $(r,c-1)$ (west), $(r,c+1)$ (east), and $(r+1,c)$ (south) all contain houses. So the forbidden configuration is a **T-tetromino** (three consecutive houses in a row, plus one house directly below the middle):

$$\text{Forbidden: } (r,c{-}1),(r,c),(r,c{+}1),(r{+}1,c)\text{ all occupied},\quad r\in[1,7],\, c\in[2,7].$$

We want the maximum number of houses with no such pattern.

## Construction achieving 50

Take rows $1$ through $7$ to be the pattern $\texttt{11011011}$ (no three consecutive 1s), and row $8$ completely full:

$$\text{row }r=\begin{cases}\texttt{11011011}&1\le r\le 7\\\texttt{11111111}&r=8\end{cases}$$

Each of rows 1–7 has 6 houses (total $7\times 6=42$); row 8 has 8. **Total = 50.**

**Validity:** A forbidden T requires three consecutive houses in some row $r\in[1,7]$ (the bar). Rows 1–7 have no three consecutive houses, so no T has its bar there. No T can be centered in row 8 (it would need row 9). Hence no house is in the shade. ✓

## Upper bound: at most 50

For a row pattern $A$, let $p(A)$ = number of houses, and let $f(A)$ = number of columns $c\in[2,7]$ where $A$ has three consecutive houses centered at $c$ (i.e., $A_{c-1}=A_c=A_{c+1}=1$).

**Key constraint.** If row $r$ has pattern $A$, then for every $c\in f(A)$, the stem cell $(r{+}1,c)$ must be empty (else the T at $(r,c)$ is forbidden). So row $r{+}1$ is forced to 0 at those $f(A)$ columns (all in $\{2,\dots,7\}$), giving
$$p_{r+1}\;\le\; 8 - f(A) = 8 - f_r.$$

**Minimal $f$ for a given popcount.** Let $g(p)=\min\{f(A):p(A)=p\}$. A run of $k$ consecutive 1s contributes $\max(0,k-2)$ centers of "111". 
- For $p\le 6$: choose a pattern with no three consecutive (e.g. $\texttt{110110}\cdots$), so $g(p)=0$.
- For $p=7$: exactly one zero splits the row into two runs of total length 7; minimizing $\max(0,a{-}2)+\max(0,7{-}a{-}2)$ over $a=0,\dots,7$ gives $g(7)=3$ (e.g. zero in position 3,4,5, or 6).
- For $p=8$: the full row has 111-centers at columns $2,\dots,7$, so $g(8)=6$.

Since $f_r\ge g(p_r)$, every pair of consecutive rows satisfies
$$p_{r+1}\le 8-g(p_r),\qquad g(p)=\begin{cases}0&p\le 6\\3&p=7\\6&p=8.\end{cases}$$

**Dynamic program.** Define $B(r,a)$ = maximum of $p_r+\cdots+p_8$ subject to $p_r\le a$ and the transition $p_{r+1}\le 8-g(p_r)$. Then
$$B(r,a)=\max_{0\le p\le a}\bigl[p+B(r{+}1,\,8-g(p))\bigr],\qquad B(8,a)=a.$$

Computing backward (using $8-g(p)=8$ for $p\le 6$, $=5$ for $p=7$, $=2$ for $p=8$):

| $r$ | $B(r,a)$ for $a\ge 6$ | (achieved by $p=6$ or $p=7$) |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | $a$ | |
| 7 | $14$ | $6+8$ |
| 6 | $20$ | $6+14$ or $7+13$ |
| 5 | $26$ | $6+20$ or $7+19$ |
| 4 | $32$ | $6+26$ or $7+25$ |
| 3 | $38$ | $6+32$ or $7+31$ |
| 2 | $44$ | $6+38$ or $7+37$ |
| 1 | $50$ | $6+44$ or $7+43$ |

At each stage, $p=8$ is dominated (it gives $8+B(r{+}1,2)$, which is smaller), and $p\le 5$ is dominated by $p=6$. The optimum is always $p=6$ or $p=7$, both giving the same value. With $p_1$ free ($a=8$):
$$B(1,8)=\max\{6+44,\;7+43,\;8+40\}=\max\{50,50,48\}=50.$$

Therefore any valid placement has **at most 50 houses**.

## Conclusion

The construction gives 50 and the upper bound proves no placement can exceed 50. The maximal number of houses is

$$\boxed{50}$$

## Setup

Index rows 1 (north) to 8 (south), columns 1 (west) to 8 (east). A house at cell $(r,c)$ is **in the shade** iff cells $(r,c-1)$ (west), $(r,c+1)$ (east), and $(r+1,c)$ (south) all contain houses. So the forbidden configuration is a **T-tetromino** (three consecutive houses in a row, plus one house directly below the middle):

$$\text{Forbidden: } (r,c{-}1),(r,c),(r,c{+}1),(r{+}1,c)\text{ all occupied},\quad r\in[1,7],\, c\in[2,7].$$

We want the maximum number of houses with no such pattern.

## Construction achieving 50

Take rows $1$ through $7$ to be the pattern $\texttt{11011011}$ (no three consecutive 1s), and row $8$ completely full:

$$\text{row }r=\begin{cases}\texttt{11011011}&1\le r\le 7\\\texttt{11111111}&r=8\end{cases}$$

Each of rows 1–7 has 6 houses (total $7\times 6=42$); row 8 has 8. **Total = 50.**

**Validity:** A forbidden T requires three consecutive houses in some row $r\in[1,7]$ (the bar). Rows 1–7 have no three consecutive houses, so no T has its bar there. No T can be centered in row 8 (it would need row 9). Hence no house is in the shade. ✓

## Upper bound: at most 50

For a row pattern $A$, let $p(A)$ = number of houses, and let $f(A)$ = number of columns $c\in[2,7]$ where $A$ has three consecutive houses centered at $c$ (i.e., $A_{c-1}=A_c=A_{c+1}=1$).

**Key constraint.** If row $r$ has pattern $A$, then for every $c\in f(A)$, the stem cell $(r{+}1,c)$ must be empty (else the T at $(r,c)$ is forbidden). So row $r{+}1$ is forced to 0 at those $f(A)$ columns (all in $\{2,\dots,7\}$), giving
$$p_{r+1}\;\le\; 8 - f(A) = 8 - f_r.$$

**Minimal $f$ for a given popcount.** Let $g(p)=\min\{f(A):p(A)=p\}$. A run of $k$ consecutive 1s contributes $\max(0,k-2)$ centers of "111". 
- For $p\le 6$: choose a pattern with no three consecutive (e.g. $\texttt{110110}\cdots$), so $g(p)=0$.
- For $p=7$: exactly one zero splits the row into two runs of total length 7; minimizing $\max(0,a{-}2)+\max(0,7{-}a{-}2)$ over $a=0,\dots,7$ gives $g(7)=3$ (e.g. zero in position 3,4,5, or 6).
- For $p=8$: the full row has 111-centers at columns $2,\dots,7$, so $g(8)=6$.

Since $f_r\ge g(p_r)$, every pair of consecutive rows satisfies
$$p_{r+1}\le 8-g(p_r),\qquad g(p)=\begin{cases}0&p\le 6\\3&p=7\\6&p=8.\end{cases}$$

**Dynamic program.** Define $B(r,a)$ = maximum of $p_r+\cdots+p_8$ subject to $p_r\le a$ and the transition $p_{r+1}\le 8-g(p_r)$. Then
$$B(r,a)=\max_{0\le p\le a}\bigl[p+B(r{+}1,\,8-g(p))\bigr],\qquad B(8,a)=a.$$

Computing backward (using $8-g(p)=8$ for $p\le 6$, $=5$ for $p=7$, $=2$ for $p=8$):

| $r$ | $B(r,a)$ for $a\ge 6$ | (achieved by $p=6$ or $p=7$) |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | $a$ | |
| 7 | $14$ | $6+8$ |
| 6 | $20$ | $6+14$ or $7+13$ |
| 5 | $26$ | $6+20$ or $7+19$ |
| 4 | $32$ | $6+26$ or $7+25$ |
| 3 | $38$ | $6+32$ or $7+31$ |
| 2 | $44$ | $6+38$ or $7+37$ |
| 1 | $50$ | $6+44$ or $7+43$ |

At each stage, $p=8$ is dominated (it gives $8+B(r{+}1,2)$, which is smaller), and $p\le 5$ is dominated by $p=6$. The optimum is always $p=6$ or $p=7$, both giving the same value. With $p_1$ free ($a=8$):
$$B(1,8)=\max\{6+44,\;7+43,\;8+40\}=\max\{50,50,48\}=50.$$

Therefore any valid placement has **at most 50 houses**.

## Conclusion

The construction gives 50 and the upper bound proves no placement can exceed 50. The maximal number of houses is

$$\boxed{50}$$
